title: The Stoic Letters, 23rd November
summary: Mind Your Mind: The letter on staying sharp in the age of AI
body_markdown:
Dear Stoics,


Around 2,400 years ago, Socrates


[worried about a dangerous new technology](https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?entryid=3894)


. He warned that it would soon plant forgetfulness in people’s souls, because they would stop exercising their memory and lean on something outside themselves. The technology he was so concerned about was… writing.


We might smile at that now, but the worry sounds more and more familiar today. Most of us ask AI for help many times a day. Sometimes the task really needs it, and sometimes we are checking something we could work out ourselves in half a minute if we just used our brains.


There is already early research on this subject, and it suggests this habit has a cost. In


[a small MIT study](https://www.media.mit.edu/publications/your-brain-on-chatgpt/)


, people who wrote essays with a chatbot showed the weakest brain connectivity of all the groups, and most of them could not quote a single line from what they had just written.


[Another study](https://doi.org/10.3390/soc15010006)


linked heavy AI use with weaker critical thinking. Researchers at Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon also


[found](https://campustechnology.com/articles/2025/02/21/study-generative-ai-could-inhibit-critical-thinking.aspx)


that the more we trust AI with a task, the less effort we put into thinking it through ourselves.


Of course, nobody is saying your brain is melting. And we’re not here to tell you to stop using AI. Our own AI mentors in Stoic exist to deepen your reflection, and they do it best when you arrive with thoughts of your own. They ask the questions we rarely think to ask ourselves and offer new perspectives inspired by great thinkers. Many of you have told us that these conversations help you understand your own entries better. Still, we thought we’d prepare a small handbook of exercises for keeping your mind in shape.


-


**Think first, ask second.**


Before you open a chatbot, give yourself two minutes. Sketch your own answer, outline or guess. Then let AI challenge it and build on it.


-


**Stay with the small questions.**


You can’t remember an actor’s name or work out how much to tip after dinner? Let your memory search for a moment. In this case, a short struggle is the exercise.


-


**Learn something by heart.**


Try to memorize a nice poem, the lyrics to your favorite songs, some good jokes, and your loved ones’ phone numbers.


-


**Do an old-school puzzle.**


In


[a trial](https://www.columbiapsychiatry.org/news/crossword-puzzles-superior-computer-video-games-slowing-memory-loss-older-adults-mild-cognitive-impairment)


with older adults who had mild memory problems, plain crosswords did more for their memory than specially designed brain games.


-


**Set a limit and go off the grid.**


Choose a daily cap or let an app blocker help you with that. Digital detoxes


[do wonders for your attention](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/4/2/pgaf017/8016017)


.


-


**Move your body.**


Your brain is part of your body and it loves a good walk. Leave the headphones at home now and then and let your thoughts wander.


-


**Ask a person.**


Next time you want a recommendation, a recipe or a second opinion, ask a friend. You will get an answer and a conversation.


-


**Write by hand.**


Forming letters with a pen


[activates far wider networks in the brain](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1219945/full)


than typing does, the kind linked to memory and learning.


It is true that the tools we use change us. As we can’t really guess how the story will continue, it is worth guarding your attention online and keeping one place where the first draft of every thought is only yours. A


[journal](https://www.newsletter.getstoic.com/p/getstoic.com/journaling)


is a good one, so write down what you think before anyone, human or machine, has a chance to chime in. Remember that your mind is still the most remarkable tool you own. Keep using it!


Yours truly,


The Stoic App Team


P.S. Fittingly, this week’s theme in the app is


*On Writing*


. More on that below.


#### I write entirely to find out what I’m thinking.


*Joan Didion*


This week, we'll explore what happens when we put ourselves into words that outlast the moment.


What does writing something down do for you? Which words of yours have stayed with you long after you wrote them? Is there a thought you have been carrying that is ready for the page?


[Open your journal](https://www.newsletter.getstoic.com/p/getstoic.com/explore/weekly-themes)


and begin with a single sentence, and the rest will follow naturally.
